newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: Russians push arms marketing drive in Abu Dhabi.
newsitem.headline: Russians push arms marketing drive in Abu Dhabi.

text.p: Russian weapons from the Kalashnikov rifle to anti-submarine mine systems drew crowds at the IDEX arms show on Tuesday, but analysts said Moscow still faced tough competition from the world's biggest arms suppliers.
The Russians have come out in force in Abu Dhabi, showing off their weapons in style at one of the largest stands at the International Defence Exhibition -- among the world's biggest arms shows.
Moscow has sent about 80 defence enterprises to the show, hoping to boost Russia's weapons sales with 500 exhibits, live weapons systems, models, brochures, booklets and videos.

"The Russian pavilion is more polished and organised this year. Now they look like all the rest," said consultant Monte Jeffery, head of a U.S. consulting firm that has joined the international rush to seek deals on the sidelines of IDEX.
Russia's top arms export agency said Moscow would by 1999 catch up with Washington, the world's chief arms supplier.

"I believe that by 1999 the volume of Russia's and the United States' arms exports will be pretty much equal, around $6.5 billion, maybe $7 (billion per year)," Alexandr Kotelkin, director general of Rosvoorouzhenie, told reporters.

"I believe we are on the right track since over just two short years we have increased our exports twofold...Last year (it made) up $3.5 billion," he said. "Our book order today stands at $8 billion. And this year we expect to conclude contracts worth $4-5 billion."
He estimated the international arms bazaar would total about $18 billion by the end of the century, with Russia and the United States each holding a third of the market.
Kotelkin said Moscow was seeking to grab 40 percent of the Gulf market by 1999.
Paul Beaver, an arms industry expert with Jane's Information Group, estimated Russia currently holds between 12 and 15 percent of the Middle East arms market, excluding Israel.
Russia's increasingly vigorous incursions into markets long the preserve of Western arms makers are causing concern from Washington to Paris to London.
In February Russia launched a new marketing drive to penetrate markets, especially in Asia, the Far East, Latin America and Arab countries.
And in Abu Dhabi, it seems Russia's efforts to outflank the United States in arms sales is paying off in the big pavilion.
Leading Russian helicopter designer Vadim Vorobiev said delegations from Yemen, Libya, Algeria and other countries came to visit his stand.
"We think the big markets will be in third world countries," he said.

In another section of the pavilion, Anwar Fancy of the American-Russian Technology Association said the future was bright for those seeking to cash in on the Russian drive to grab a bigger market share.

"There are many opportunities here," said Fancy, who is trying to help the Russians turn military industries into viable commercial projects. "Visitors from 21 countries like Kuwait, Egypt, Syria and Oman came to see us and five want to sit down at the negotiating table."
But Beaver expressed doubt that the Russians would catch up with the Americans by 1999.
"I don't think it will happen. They have to prove they are reliable suppliers and a lot depends on the level of uncertainty in the world and also stability at home," he said.
